query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high‐entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is governed by the formation of a stable, nanocrystalline oxide layer that develops either during service or can be pre-engineered, which reduces friction and material removal during abrasive contact.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited HEA coating with minimal surface oxide formation
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., heating in a controlled oxygen atmosphere) to form a uniform, nanocrystalline oxide layer on the coating surface
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted under identical sliding/abrasion conditions at moderate temperatures (e.g., room temperature to ≈100°C) where the oxide layer remains stable
generation.structural_mediator: The thickness, continuity, and crystallinity of the nanocrystalline oxide film at the surface
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed nanocrystalline oxide layer acts as a protective barrier, reducing direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding or impact stresses and thereby lowering friction and wear. This layer provides improved resistance to material removal via abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical wear conditions, coatings modified by the controlled oxidation treatment will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to as-deposited (baseline) samples.
generation.baseline: As-deposited HEA coatings without any pre-oxidation treatment
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold within wear regimes where the applied load and temperature do not cause spallation or breakdown of the protective oxide layer; if wear conditions exceed these limits, the oxide may fail to provide protection.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum oxide thickness and microstructural characteristics (e.g., grain size, phase composition) that maximize wear resistance may vary with HEA composition and service conditions, and further work is needed to establish these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coating samples: one set is subjected to a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to generate a uniform nanocrystalline oxide layer, while the second set remains in the as-deposited state. Conduct identical sliding/abrasion wear tests (e.g., using a ball-on-disk tribometer) on both sets under the same load and temperature conditions.
measurements: Measure friction coefficients during wear tests using the tribometer.
Quantify wear rates by profilometry or mass loss measurements after testing.
Characterize the oxide layer (thickness, continuity, crystallinity) using TEM or XPS depth profiling before and after wear tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficients and wear rates—i.e., no observable performance improvement compared to the as-deposited samples—or if the oxide layer is found to degrade or spall irreversibly under the test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.
